title: Haredi party withholds backing from Netanyahu as Eisenkot leads Israel PM recommendations
dek: United Torah Judaism recommended no one in President Herzog's consultations, leaving opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot ahead as Herzog weighs who gets the first try at forming a government.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party declined on Thursday to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu, or anyone else, for prime minister, as President Isaac Herzog finished two days of consultations on who should get the first chance to form Israel's next government. The party had backed Netanyahu after each of the previous five elections, RTE reported.

The move leaves opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief who heads the Yashar party, ahead in recommendations. The Jerusalem Post reported that Eisenkot was positioned to receive the mandate once the talks ended on Thursday evening; Herzog had not announced his decision by 9 pm IST.

## What happened

UTJ met Herzog first on Thursday morning. "We came to discuss topics and not people," its lawmaker Yitzhak Pindrus said, according to The Jerusalem Post. The party's Degel HaTorah faction, which holds four of its seven seats, said on Wednesday it would recommend no one, on instructions from its rabbis, The Times of Israel reported. The paper described the decision as a sign of the rift with Netanyahu over his government's failure to pass a law exempting religious seminary students from military service. Pindrus said the party's priority was "sorting out the status of Torah students", RTE reported.

Also on Thursday, the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan, and the Arab-led Ra'am party of Mansour Abbas recommended Eisenkot. Abbas told Herzog his party supports fully disarming Hamas, The Jerusalem Post reported. The far-right Otzma Yehudit party of Itamar Ben-Gvir recommended Netanyahu, and its delegation repeated claims that the election was stolen. The Joint List, the other Arab-led list, said it would also recommend Eisenkot, Al Jazeera reported. Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad, Yashar and Netanyahu's Likud were due to meet Herzog later in the day.

On Wednesday the Religious Zionist Party, Shas and Zehut recommended Netanyahu, while Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu backed Eisenkot.

## The numbers

Final results give Netanyahu's bloc 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats, the opposition camp 48, and the Arab-led lists 19, so no side has the 61 needed for a majority. The Times of Israel expected Eisenkot to end the consultations with at least 56 recommendations to Netanyahu's 53 or fewer. With both Arab-led lists backing him, his total is expected to reach 67, Al Jazeera reported, a majority of the house.

Recommendations are not the same as a coalition. Eisenkot and his allies have said they will not form a government with the Arab-led parties, and Liberman could walk away if Eisenkot relied on their support, RTE reported. Several of his partners also oppose sitting with the ultra-Orthodox parties.

## Netanyahu's response

Netanyahu said in a video that there were "serious suspicions" that foreign powers had funded the election and questioned the loyalty of Arab citizens, RTE reported. Israel's Central Elections Committee certified the results on Wednesday and said it had found no evidence of fraud.

## What happens next

Herzog is not bound to choose the candidate with the most recommendations. Whoever receives the mandate has 28 days to form a government, which can be extended by 14. The new Knesset is sworn in on 10 November.

For India, which has close defence, technology and trade ties with Israel, the outcome will shape Israeli policy on the stalled Gaza ceasefire and on Iran. Eisenkot has warned against a new war with Iran, which matters to India because of the risk to oil supplies and Indian seafarers in the Strait of Hormuz.
